visible

/VIZ-uh-buhl/ · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Visible means able to be seen.

From the top of the tower, the entire coastline was clearly visible for miles in every direction.

Example

On the clearest nights of the year, when the city finally cuts enough streetlights during a planned outage, thousands of stars that are normally lost to light pollution become visible to the naked eye all at once.

The stars were always there — city lights simply overpowered them. Removing that interference is all it took to make them visible again, which is exactly the word's simple, literal meaning: able to be seen.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

observable: Observable emphasizes that something can be watched or studied directly, and it carries a scientific flavor — observable symptoms, observable behavior. Visible makes the plainer, smaller claim that a thing can be seen at all, with no suggestion of study.

detectable: Detectable means able to be picked up at all — often faintly, and often by instruments or tests rather than the eye. Visible is specifically about ordinary sight: if you can see it unaided, it is visible, whether or not any instrument could find more.

conspicuous: Conspicuous — taught on its own card in this unit — means standing out and drawing attention. Visible is far weaker: merely able to be seen. Everything conspicuous is visible, but an ordinary mailbox you pass every day is visible without being conspicuous at all.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

invisible: the direct opposite — unable to be seen at all

hidden: deliberately or accidentally kept out of sight

Where it sits · how easily the eye picks it up

perceptible → visible → apparent

perceptible vs. visible: Something perceptible might be just barely detectable, at the edge of what the eye can register — well short of plainly visible.

apparent vs. visible: Something apparent goes beyond merely visible — not just able to be seen but obvious; the word suits conclusions and inner states that show themselves, more than physical objects simply sitting in view.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — vis-: to see (Latin videre/vis-)

Suffix — -ible: capable of being

Put it together: "visible" literally means "capable of being seen" — the vis- root, from Latin videre, "to see," is one of the most productive roots in English, appearing in dozens of words about sight and observation.

Use the root in a new word: vision: After the surgery, her vision was sharper than it had been in twenty years.

Root Check

Word Choice

neutral, literal or figurative

Visible is mostly literal (able to be physically seen), but it also appears figuratively, as in 'a visible improvement' or 'no visible means of support,' where it means clearly evident rather than literally seen with the eyes.
